findings.detail: The `stage-release` and `publish-release` jobs first run "Resolve env-specific secrets", which appends the R2 access key, R2 secret, endpoint and (in `publish-release`) `release_key` and `coordinator_url` to `$GITHUB_ENV`. Every later step in the job therefore inherits them. The next step, "Install publication tools", runs `pip install awscli` from PyPI. The version is unpinned, there are no hashes, and it is a fresh venv. A compromised or typosquatted awscli dependency, or a malicious sdist build script, could run code that reads the release key, R2 secrets and the job's GITHUB_TOKEN. In `publish-release` the job has no `permissions:` block, so it inherits `contents: write`. With the release key an attacker can register an arbitrary binary or CodeDirectory hash with the coordinator (A-005, A-011). They could also overwrite the staged bundle in R2 before publication, after the signing and notarization checks. Fix: pin awscli and its dependencies by hash, or use a preinstalled or vendored tool. Run the install before secrets are exported to `$GITHUB_ENV`, and pass secrets only through step-level `env:` on the single publish step. Give `publish-release` explicit least-privilege `permissions:` (`contents: read`, `actions: read`).
findings.title: Unpinned `pip install awscli` runs with R2 write credentials and the coordinator release key in the job environment

findings.detail: In publish-release, the 'Resolve env-specific secrets' step appends r2_secret_access_key, release_key and coordinator_url to $GITHUB_ENV (lines 1140-1155). The next steps then run `pip install awscli` into a fresh venv with no version or hash pinning (line 1174). The same pattern appears in stage-release at line 1059, where R2 keys are exported. Every GitHub Action in this workflow is pinned by SHA, but this PyPI install is not. A compromised or typosquatted awscli or dependency release would execute with RELEASE_KEY and R2 write keys in its environment. The attacker could then register a malicious binary hash with the coordinator (A-005, A-011), overwrite release objects in R2, or publish aliases. The base-side workflow is not visible in the supplied patch, so I cannot tell whether this install is new. Fix: install from a hash-pinned requirements file with `--require-hashes`, or use a pinned preinstalled CLI. Also install the tools before secrets are exported to GITHUB_ENV, and pass secrets only to the single step that needs them.
findings.title: Unpinned `pip install awscli` runs in publish job after release key and R2 credentials are exported

findings.detail: The base release-swift.yml ran a `resolve-env` job first. It checked out `master` and ran `provider-release-resume.py verify-source` before any signing or publishing credential was used, so a candidate branch's policy could not authorize secrets. The head replaces all jobs with a call to `./.github/workflows/release-provider.yml`. That call hard-codes `environment: prod`, forwards `validation_only` and `version_override`, and uses `secrets: inherit`, which passes every repository secret (Apple signing cert, provisioning profile, PROD/DEV/STAGING R2 keys, release key). A local reusable workflow resolves at the triggering ref, and a `workflow_dispatch` on a non-master branch is allowed with `environment == 'prod'`. If release-provider.yml lacks an equivalent reviewed-source gate, a branch writer could obtain the A-005 release API key and Developer ID signing material, and register a build in A-011. That would weaken T-034 and T-013. The base also confined `validation_only` to dev; the head forwards it alongside `environment: prod`. The new file is not in this diff, so this cannot be confirmed. Fix: confirm release-provider.yml still verifies the source against master before any secret-consuming job, reject `validation_only` combined with prod, and replace `secrets: inherit` with an explicit allowlist of secrets.
findings.title: Release signing now delegates to a reusable workflow with `secrets: inherit` and a hard-coded prod environment; the source-trust gate is not visible
